And we got something to eat, and after we got to his office, you know, and he started talking to us, explaining --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: ALLAN ASBJORN KNUDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- what we could do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you believe that, or do you have an idea that you were treated any differently than anyone else who would enter the parliament building?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN ASBJORN KNUDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say yes. We were foreigners. If you got to the parliament at that time, there was going to be roadblocks along it. My opinion was it's not just a place you could get in, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You testified that on the Exhibit P241.1, which was a certificate of November 5, 1993, you testified that you actually saw Mario Milicevic sign that document. Was that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN ASBJORN KNUDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my testimony, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did you also see him type out that certificate?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN ASBJORN KNUDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by "type out"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: With a typewriter.

utterances.speaker: ALLAN ASBJORN KNUDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So basically, is it your testimony that the certificate, the typed certificate, was already prepared and then you just observed the signature?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN ASBJORN KNUDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had been prepared for us, and it was ready for us. And later on, they got a photo, and we were supposed to have these plastic badges -- actually, we never received anyone. They told us it was just a temporary paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Then on Exhibit P658, which was an October 22, 1993 letter -- do you recall that document? Do you recall that document? If not, I will have the usher show you that document.

utterances.speaker: ALLAN ASBJORN KNUDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a lot of documents. I would like to see it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I apologise. I know you did. I'm just trying to move as quickly as possible here.

utterances.speaker: ALLAN ASBJORN KNUDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: For the record, you're looking at that document P658 now?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN ASBJORN KNUDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You recall -- were you present when this Branko Barbic signed that document?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN ASBJORN KNUDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did he prepare it in your presence?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN ASBJORN KNUDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not. He asked the secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. You turned over all of the documents that you had in your possession to the Danish police when you were first interviewed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN ASBJORN KNUDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, yes, to my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And was there -- if you know, was there any reason that an individual from the Danish criminal police sat with you in this interview in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN ASBJORN KNUDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a Danish rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It is a Danish rule?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN ASBJORN KNUDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's because in 1997, I think it was a Danish guy who interviewed me, and 1998 was a Portuguese police officer came to Denmark to ask me, and then there had to be a Danish policeman nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And that was because, to your knowledge, Danish law requires it?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN ASBJORN KNUDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told so, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. That's the only questions that I have. For the record, because I was admonished at 2.30 by Judge Clark, I don't believe I started my cross-examination until 3.00. Thank you very much. Thank you, Witness. It's nice for you to come and give your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from judges? Judge Clark?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I have just one question. Mr. Knudsen, when you were injured and taken to the hospital in Mostar, were you an in-patient there? Did you sleep overnight?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN ASBJORN KNUDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I slept overnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: How was the hospital functioning? Was it operating as a normal hospital, or was it a hospital that was managing on a shoestring and with limited facilities?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN ASBJORN KNUDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say with limited facilities. You would have small beds standing nearby each other, even with hard wounded and slightly wounded. And if there was a problem -- we had an occasion one guy died, they would take this small tent, roll him around the bed so you couldn't see him. That was my expression of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Did you see any of the prisoners being brought in and treated?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN ASBJORN KNUDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Judge Diarra?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. Witness, I have a question for you. As regards the mistreatment to which prisoners were subjected, you spoke about bottles on the head and the opening of fire by guards, and you also mentioned military court and summary -- simulated war crime tribunals. Mr. Martinovic, was he -- was it possible for him to be informed of the mistreatment to which prisoners were subjected? Was he aware of that at the time that mistreatment was being done? Or was he ever informed by anyone else of such mistreatment? Martinovic and Naletilic, could they be -- was it possible that they were aware of such cases of mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN ASBJORN KNUDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible they had been told later, perhaps, but my impression when these things happened, it was occasionally when the Croatians got drunk, that things started to happen. Like, one occasion was this with the bottles was because we were sleeping in the apartment at the base and a lot of rounds getting fire, and one guy got out, you know, and came back to us and sounded like madmen, they were drunk, the Croatians, so they picked up the prisoners who was in -- up in the ceiling of the house - they were kept there - and lined two of them up and put bottles on their head and went back shooting to hit the bottles. So that was my impression: Was these people got drunk or anything and they had the power to do so, they did it. But if they'd been told later, Stela or Naletilic, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of judges' questions? Yes, Mr. Par? Further-cross-examined by Mr. Par:

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Mr. Knudsen, about this incident you just mentioned involving bottles on top of heads, did that happen during the -- those ten days you spent in the Vinko Skrobo unit or in some other place?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN ASBJORN KNUDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened in Ljubuski. It was not in Vinko Skrobo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for helping us by giving your evidence. The usher will show you out of the room. We wish you good luck in your future.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, are there any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The following documents I would like to tender as evidence: P594, P14.4, P14.5, P241.1, P606, P658. The document P004 [sic] has already been tendered before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Your Honour. I would also like to tender some evidence on behalf of the Defence, the map, 14.5, and I would like the Registry to give me a number for that. Then P608, again asking for the number, for a number. And also I would like to tender, on behalf of the Defence, the original signature of Vinko Martinovic after the judge's suggestion this morning to tender it as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you show this signature to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You have to show them right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do that now, and I would like to note that an uncontested signature of Vinko Martinovic is available at the detention unit where it is kept. If I may ask the usher's assistance in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. giving this paper to Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would object, Your Honour, because there was some ruling rendered by the Trial Chamber about the order in which documents should be rendered, and the parties should be warned in advance and given an opportunity of seeing the documents. We have not seen them before. And now, what is the origin of this document? Where was it received? How? In what circumstances? Difficult circumstances? Was this signature made or not? I don't know. And then there is special -- a specific order of taking, removing samples for comparative examination and graphic expertise. I think that -- I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do allow me to respond. I believe that during my cross-examination before offering this document, I said clearly, and I'll repeat it now, that during the examination-in-chief of this witness, who claimed about one signature, that it was made by my client in his presence, and after that I asked my client to sign a blank paper. That's the origin of the signature I'm trying to present. The second issue is that this was about to be shown to a witness who is not an expert, but the only reason that we used this document in the way that we used this is to help the Chamber attach appropriate weight to certain evidence. There was no ulterior motive or tactics designed in not showing the Prosecution something that I should have. It was only to -- designed to help verify this signature, and the Prosecutor's office will be able to authenticate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Those documents that are not objected, opposed by both parties, are admitted into the evidence. As for the signature, after consultations among the Judges, we'll admit it into the evidence. It is so decided. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, you were busy with that conversation, and I would just, for the record, state that on Exhibit P658, since the witness testified both documents that have this Branko Barbic signature, we wouldn't object to the admission of those documents at this time because of the witness's testimony. However, we would ask that the weight to be given those documents at the end of the trial after we have our witnesses be evaluated at that time due to differences in Croatian law and the parliament, which we will bring forth at the time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If this document is not admitted, how could we give any weight to this document at this stage? My suggestion is that we have this document admitted into the evidence. And later on, when your case comes, you could present your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I would like to give the numbers to all these admitted exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They are PP594, PP14.4/3, PP14.5/8, PP241.1, PP606, PP658, DD2/16. That is for the marked P14.5. And DD2/17 for this Document 608. And then DD2/18 is the note for the signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. This Trial Chamber is seized of this motion filed by the Prosecution on the matter of the protective measures concerning the next witness. We'll render our decisions this afternoon. We'll adjourn until 9.30 tomorrow morning.
